claims.text: SQUID magnetometry combined with magnetic susceptibility measurements can detect the presence of ferromagnetic ground states.
The proposed specimen is a single-crystal ferromagnetic material with a well-defined crystal structure and minimal defects.
The specimen is cooled near 0 K in a controlled magnetic-field environment.
A magnetic field between 0 and 100 Oe is applied during SQUID magnetometry.
An applied magnetic field causes the material's magnetic moments to align.
Magnetic moments align more easily in a ferromagnetic material than in a non-ferromagnetic material.
Alignment of magnetic moments produces a measurable change in magnetic susceptibility.
Spontaneous magnetization can be detected through magnetic susceptibility measurements.
Applying the field will produce a 20% increase in magnetic susceptibility relative to the zero-field baseline at 0 K.
Operating between 0 and 10 K minimizes thermal fluctuations and ensures that the material is in its ground state.
A field range of 0–100 Oe avoids saturation while still inducing a measurable response.
Defects, impurities, and SQUID instrumental errors may affect the accuracy of the predicted susceptibility change.
The hypothesis is falsified if the susceptibility increase is less than 10% relative to baseline or if the no-field control shows an increase greater than 5%.
